22 Two particles in a progressive wave are a distance 10 cm apart. The two graphs show the
variation with time t of the displacement d of the two particles.

What could be represented by the two graphs?
A
particles in a longitudinal wave with a compression and the nearest rarefaction separated by
10 cm
B
particles in a longitudinal wave with a compression and the nearest rarefaction separated by
20 cm
C
particles in a transverse wave with a peak and the nearest trough separated by 20 cm
D
particles in a transverse wave with two adjacent peaks separated by 10 cm

hints: Compare the two $d$ against $t$ graphs at the same instant: when the left graph is at maximum positive $d$, the right graph is at maximum negative $d$.
Opposite displacements at all times means antiphase, a phase difference of $180^{\circ}$ or half a cycle, so the 10 cm separation must equal $\lambda/2$.
Recall that nearest compression to rarefaction and nearest peak to trough are both $\lambda/2$ apart, while adjacent peaks or compressions are $\lambda$ apart - check which distance equals 10 cm.
walkthrough: Look at $t=0$: the left particle starts at $+d_{max}$ while the right particle starts near $-d_{max}$. At every later $t$ one is positive when the other is negative, so they oscillate in antiphase.
Antiphase means phase difference $= 180^{\circ} = \pi \text{ rad}$, which corresponds to a path separation of half a wavelength: $\Delta x = \lambda/2$.
Here $\Delta x = 10 \text{ cm}$, so $\lambda/2 = 10 \text{ cm}$ and $\lambda = 20 \text{ cm}$.

In a longitudinal wave, a compression and the nearest rarefaction are opposite states of the oscillation, separated by $\lambda/2$. A separation of 10 cm therefore matches $\lambda/2 = 10 \text{ cm}$.

Options with $\lambda = 40 \text{ cm}$ would make 10 cm only $\lambda/4$, and adjacent peaks 10 cm apart would make the particles in phase. Only compression to nearest rarefaction 10 cm apart gives antiphase. This is option A.

A.explanation: The graphs are in antiphase, so 10 cm is half a wavelength. Compression to nearest rarefaction is also half a wavelength, so 10 cm fits.

B.explanation: Compression to rarefaction of 20 cm means $\lambda = 40 \text{ cm}$, so 10 cm would be only a quarter wavelength, not antiphase.

C.explanation: Peak to nearest trough of 20 cm means $\lambda = 40 \text{ cm}$, so 10 cm would give a $90^{\circ}$ phase difference, not opposite motion.

D.explanation: Adjacent peaks 10 cm apart means $\lambda = 10 \text{ cm}$, so particles 10 cm apart would be in phase with identical $d$-$t$ graphs.
